"Northern Territory police failed to act on a string of self-harm and suicide attempts in caged police vehicles before the death of a vulnerable 23-year-old man last year, a coroner has found. NT coroner Greg Cavanagh has criticised police for failing to act on an internal report recommending CCTV cameras be installed in caged vehicles in 2013, following an earlier death in custody. In the three years between the two deaths, there were at least 16 attempted suicides in caged vehicles.

“In six cases the persons were not detected until they were semi-conscious or unconscious,” Cavanagh found. “It wasn’t a matter of if a person would die in the back of a police van but when.”

On 16 September last year, two officers were making their way through Darwin, on their way to investigate a noise complaint, when they came across the scene of a serious crash. A Toyota Hilux had smashed into a palm tree on the corner of the Stuart Highway and Bagot Road, not far from Darwin airport.

Hiding behind some vegetation was Dale Scott Walkinshaw, 23. Walkinshaw was unharmed but held his passenger in his arms. The young woman, whom he had met earlier at a bar, was in and out of consciousness, having suffered an injury to her back. Walkinshaw was well over the limit, returning a reading of 0.149.

What followed, the coroner found, was a chain of decisions and entrenched practices that left a clearly distressed young man alone and unwatched in the back of a caged police truck for more than 10 minutes, despite repeated warnings over several years that such an outcome was almost inevitable.

Paramedics arrived shortly after the officers and took over treatment of the injured woman, who was transported to Royal Darwin hospital. She survived her injuries. With the immediate medical emergency under control, attention turned to Walkinshaw.

He was described in police statements and body-worn camera footage as pale, shaking and intermittently crying. Witnesses recalled him asking several times whether the woman was going to die and whether he would “go to jail forever”. Officers at the scene noted he smelled strongly of alcohol and slurred his words.

After failing a roadside breath test, Walkinshaw was placed under arrest for driving under the influence and taken to the rear of the caged police vehicle. According to the evidence heard at the inquest, he was not violent or combative, but “highly emotional” and “despondent”.

Several bystanders gave evidence that they heard him say words to the effect of “I can’t do this” and “I don’t want to live anymore” as he was escorted to the vehicle. One witness, a local resident who had come out of his house after hearing the crash, told the court he saw Walkinshaw briefly resist being placed in the cage and then slump against the metal wall, sobbing.

Despite these signs, the officers closed the metal doors and left him alone while they remained at the scene to assist with traffic control and paperwork. The inquest heard that this was “standard practice” in Darwin – a practice that had been specifically identified as dangerous in an internal review three years earlier.

Inside the dark, confined space of the caged compartment, there was no CCTV camera, no audio recording and no direct line of sight from the front of the vehicle. The only way to check on a prisoner was to physically leave the front seat, walk to the rear and open the hatch.

About eight minutes after Walkinshaw was secured in the cage, another officer arrived. He later told the court he heard “thumping” noises from the back of the vehicle but assumed the prisoner was “kicking off” in frustration. No one opened the van to look.

Cavanagh found that in that period Walkinshaw used his T-shirt and the metal grill to attempt to hang himself. When officers finally opened the door, preparing to transport him to the watch house for a formal breath analysis, they found him unresponsive, slumped forward with fabric around his neck.

One officer yelled for assistance while another fumbled with the knots. An ambulance was called and CPR commenced on the road beside the paddy wagon, under the glow of streetlights and the intermittent flash of police beacons. Walkinshaw was rushed to hospital but could not be revived. He was pronounced dead a short time later.

In his formal findings handed down in Darwin’s local court, Cavanagh was blunt in his assessment of systemic failure.

“The NT police force was on notice – and had been on notice for several years – that detainees in caged vehicles presented an acute and known risk of self-harm,” he said. “Yet the organisation failed to implement simple, practical measures that would have cost comparatively little and saved a life.”

The inquest heard that after the 2013 death in custody – in which another man had used clothing to attempt self-strangulation in a police vehicle – an internal safety review recommended the installation of CCTV cameras in all caged vehicles, the introduction of routine visual checks every five minutes, and clearer guidance on the management of intoxicated and distressed detainees.

Internal correspondence tendered to the court showed that while senior officers “agreed in principle” with the recommendations, they were repeatedly deferred due to “budgetary pressures” and “competing operational priorities”. Cavanagh described these justifications as “wholly inadequate”.

“The cost of installing CCTV cameras is modest when weighed against the cost of a coronial inquest, a human life and the ongoing trauma to a family,” he said. “The decision to place fiscal considerations above detainee safety was misguided and, in the circumstances, negligent.”

Walkinshaw’s mother, who sat through the entire inquest clutching a small framed photograph of her son as a boy, broke down as the coroner described his final moments. Outside court she said she hoped no other family would have to “get that knock on the door” because someone had been left alone in a cage.

“My boy wasn’t perfect. He made a mistake that night, a big one, and he’d have to live with that if he’d survived,” she said. “But he should have had the chance to live with it. He should have been watched, cared for, treated like a human being. Instead they locked him in a box and walked away.”

The NT police commissioner, Michael Murphy, issued a brief statement following the findings, saying the force “acknowledged the coroner’s concerns” and offered “sincere condolences” to Walkinshaw’s family. He confirmed that since Walkinshaw’s death, NT police had begun rolling out CCTV cameras in caged vehicles and introduced new procedures for monitoring at-risk detainees.

However, under questioning at the inquest, senior police conceded that even after multiple suicide attempts in the back of vans – including instances where detainees were found unconscious – there had been “no sense of urgency” about implementing reforms.

Cavanagh said this culture of complacency was central to his concerns.

“This was not an unforeseeable tragedy, nor was it a one-off oversight,” he said. “The history of prior incidents demonstrates a pattern: warnings were given, reports were written, recommendations were made. And then very little changed on the ground.”

He made a series of formal recommendations, including:

• Mandatory CCTV coverage in all caged police vehicles within 12 months  
• A requirement that all detained persons identified as distressed, intoxicated or potentially suicidal be transported in vehicles where they can be directly observed by officers  
• Written protocols for physical checks on detainees at intervals no greater than five minutes when they are left in vehicles  
• Training for officers in recognising and responding to signs of acute psychological distress.

Cavanagh also recommended that all previous incidents of self-harm in police vehicles over the past five years be reviewed by an independent body, with a view to identifying further systemic failings.

Civil liberties advocates said the case highlighted longstanding concerns about the treatment of detainees in the Northern Territory, particularly Aboriginal people, who are disproportionately represented in custody statistics. While Walkinshaw was not Aboriginal, lawyers and community groups argued that the same systemic failures that contributed to his death had already done disproportionate harm in Indigenous communities.

“We have been warning for years about the lethal combination of cages, invisibility and indifference,” said one advocate. “If a person is out of sight, they are too often out of mind. And in custody, that can be a death sentence.”

For Walkinshaw’s family, the coroner’s words provided some measure of official acknowledgment but little comfort. His mother said she would remember her son not as “the drunk driver in the headlines” but as “the cheeky kid who loved fishing and always rang me to ask how to cook his dinner properly”.

“I can accept that he did the wrong thing getting behind the wheel,” she said quietly. “What I can’t accept is that once he was in their care, there was no care at all.”"
